transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-08-05 14:00 PDT
Duration: ~78 mins
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Eric Huang (Redwood SE), Marcos De la Cruz (Redwood), Dr. Priya Anand (CTO, Galena Bio), Luis Romero (Platform), Marta Kovacevic (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated): SE walked through topology and root-cause hypotheses for intermittent p99 spikes seen in Galena's prod workload. Discussed KV cache sharding, routing, batching windows, streaming vs non-streaming behavior, and quantization edge-cases.

[00:00] Samira Patel: Hey everybody, thanks for carving out time. we're going to jump in, Eric's going to drive the technical bits, i'll surface some commercial constraints at the end. Priya, Luis, Marta, you good on time?

[00:08] Dr. Priya Anand: Yeah we're good. we pushed out of the morning and this window works. we saw a couple of those p99 blips last week and wanted to understand whether it's networking or your runtime, and when to expect dedicated vs hosted decisions.

[00:18] Eric Huang: Awesome. quick context from our side: we got your traffic histogram and the two sample prompts you sent. looks like median request tokens around 32, but a fat tail up to 512 tokens for some long-form summarization jobs, so that's an important detail for batching and kv cache behavior.

[00:34] Luis Romero: yep, those long tail jobs are the pain. p95 is fine at ~75ms for short requests, but p99 jumps to 350-420ms during 2-3 hour daily windows.

[00:45] Eric Huang: okay that matches a couple hypotheses. first: multi-hop. if any request traverses cross-region VPC peering or goes through a central proxy (Envoy) it can add non-deterministic 30-60ms hop latency which amplifies at p99. second: kv cache misses and shard hot-spots — if the prefix isn't in-memory we fetch from remote node, adds 80-200ms depending on serialization and protobuf overhead.

[01:06] Marta Kovacevic: to be clear, we run a hybrid topology: inference in our on-prem racks for PHI-sensitive workloads but burst to Redwood hosted in us-west for peak traffic. we also have a shared KV cluster in a single AZ right now.

[01:18] Eric Huang: that explains it. single-AZ KV cluster is a common hotspot. small amount of cross-az routing during bursting introduces tail variance.

[01:26] Marcos De la Cruz: if I can interject— the runtime supports multi-level caching: local prefix cache, node-local KV, and remote kv. our metrics show p50->p90 benefits dramatically when prefix cache hits. but p99 is driven by cold cache walks and remote fetches.

[01:40] Dr. Priya Anand: so streaming vs non-streaming — we saw that streaming sometimes closes earlier but we also saw more p99 jitter. why would streaming increase spikes?

[01:49] Eric Huang: good question. streaming changes end-to-end backpressure: with streaming each token can be flush-through, but if any downstream consumer (proxy, edge) buffers or reshapes TCP windows you'll see batching windows collapse and more head-of-line blocking. in other words, streaming reduces per-token latency for happy-path, but it exposes any network instability to every token. for our runtime, we also do continuous batching — streaming requests may get smaller aggregate batches, raising per-token cost during busy times and increasing variance.

[02:18] Luis Romero: hmm, that aligns. when we forced non-streaming (collect full generation before return) the p99 was more stable but overall tail latency was slightly higher for longer sequences.

[02:27] Eric Huang: exactly. non-streaming lets the runtime form larger batches and amortize kernel launch overhead, so p99 can be more stable if you tune the batching window. but it increases time-to-first-byte for long outputs. it's always a tradeoff: user-visible latency vs system-level variance.

[02:44] Marta Kovacevic: can you explain kv shard hot-spotting? we have some prompts that generate a lot of identical prefixes — could that be the issue?

[02:52] Eric Huang: yes. if many concurrent requests reference the same prefix entry the node owning that shard becomes a hot-shelf. we saw cases where a single hot key accounted for 30% of remote kv fetches during a spike. typical mitigations: 1) consistent hashing with virtual nodes to spread ownership, 2) active replication of top-N hot keys to multiple nodes (sync or async), 3) local pre-warm — on model load or traffic ramp we prime the prefix cache for expected hot keys.

[03:23] Dr. Priya Anand: replication sounds good but how much memory would that cost? we have tight RAM on on-prem nodes.

[03:29] Eric Huang: replication increases memory proportional to number of replicated keys and their embedding sizes. for prefix caches the entries are often small (token sequences + metadata), so replicating top 100-500 keys might be a reasonable tradeoff. we recommended a heatmap-based approach: monitor top-1000 keys by QPS, then replicate top-100 only.

[03:47] Marcos De la Cruz: also worth to highlight the serialization format: we support compact msgpack and also a gzip+protobuf path. msgpack is cheaper CPU but less dense, protobuf gz is denser but CPU heavier on decode — which matters if fetches are on CPU constrained nodes. sometimes folks pick the denser format thinking it reduces network, but end up CPU-throttling during bursts which shows as p99 spikes.

[04:12] Luis Romero: we use protobuf gzip today. maybe that explains the CPU tail.

[04:16] Eric Huang: yeah that could be it. quick note on quantization: running int8/4 quantized models reduces memory and improves throughput, but cold-start compilation or kernel selection can add an initial 80-120ms on first inference path for certain layers. if your workload has many rare long-form jobs, those cold paths show up at p99.

[04:36] Dr. Priya Anand: are there automatic fallbacks? like if a quantized backend is slower for some sequences, will the runtime switch to float32?

[04:44] Eric Huang: currently we have policy-driven fallbacks: you can prefer quantized with a latency threshold, and if the runtime measures degradation above that threshold it can route to a float path. but switching has costs; we typically recommend canarying and using a small float fleet as warm fallback.

[04:59] Samira Patel: Priya, you asked about when dedicated makes sense — from a latency consistency viewpoint, Dedicated with local KV and pinned capacity reduces p99 variance because you control placement. but it's a commercial commitment — we'll map costs on the next step.

[05:12] Luis Romero: can you walk through an example of how network hops amplify variance? we have VPC transit in our topology that might add a proxy in-between.

[05:20] Eric Huang: sure. imagine a 3-hop path: client -> customer proxy (Envoy) -> centralized KV -> inference node. each hop has base latency + jitter. p99 is not additive in mean, it's additive in tail percentiles in a sense: when each hop has its own tail, the product of tail probabilities creates rare but large spikes. For example, a 10ms jitter at hop A and 20ms at hop B might coincide rarely producing a 200ms spike. We mitigate by reducing hops (direct peering), co-locating KV, or doing asynchronous fetches for non-blocking prefix data.

[06:02] Marta Kovacevic: asynchronous fetches — what does that mean for correctness? our generation depends on prefixes for token probability.

[06:09] Eric Huang: there are two models: 1) blocking prefix fetch before generation (strong correctness), 2) speculative generation with best-effort prefix and repair later — the latter reduces p99 but needs application-level reconciliation. depends on whether the prefix materially changes output quality.

[06:26] Luis Romero: we can't accept inconsistent answers for medical abstracts; so probably blocking.

[06:31] Eric Huang: understood. for blocking paths, you want to guarantee prefix local hits as much as possible. network-wise that means either local KV in the same AZ/cluster or replicating key sets.

[06:42] Marcos De la Cruz: also batching window tuning: we expose two knobs — target latency window (ms) and max batch size. if you set window to 20ms and traffic is bursty, small batches may form often and increase per-token kernel overhead. if you increase to 60-80ms you get better throughput but higher time-to-first-token. in practice teams pick 30-40ms for balanced SLOs.

[07:06] Dr. Priya Anand: is there a way to make batching adaptive per-route? some routes are short chat, others are long summarization.

[07:12] Eric Huang: yes route-level policies are supported — each route can have its own batching window, model variant, and cache policy. you can also set an admission controller to prioritize low-latency routes during bursts.

[07:23] Luis Romero: about metrics — what traces do we need to give you so you can reproduce p99 in your lab?

[07:28] Eric Huang: best is: 1) seq-length histogram, 2) request timestamps + route IDs for a representative 24 hour window, 3) top-k prefix heatmap, 4) VPC topology and peering diagram, 5) Envoy/proxy timeouts and retries. with that we can replay in our stress harness.

[07:46] Samira Patel: we'll use that to scope a short PoC: host a dedicated small fleet, replicate top-100 prefixes, and run a 24-hour synthetic replay to show p95/p99 improvement.

[07:55] Marta Kovacevic: one more question — HSM/KMS and audit logs: when we burst to hosted, can we keep KMS on our side?

[08:02] Eric Huang: yes — we support customer-managed KMS via key wraps; you can keep master keys in your HSM — Redwood stores wrapped keys, and audit logs are forwarded to your SIEM. there may be a small increase in latency on key unwrap path but that's usually <10ms and can be batched.

[08:19] Luis Romero: what about SSO and SAML? we need RBAC mappings for model access and cost tracking per project.

[08:25] Samira Patel: we support SAML/SSO and SCIM provisioning, plus token-level tagging for cost breakdowns. we'll include the security pack docs after this call.

[08:34] Dr. Priya Anand: great. i'd like to dig into one concrete scenario — during last week's incident p99 spiked to 415ms for a period of 12 minutes. we saw no CPU saturation. what should we look at in traces?

[08:46] Eric Huang: look for increases in remote kv latencies, RPC retries, proxy 5xxs, and sudden batch size shrinkages. often CPU flatlines but RPC queues fill up which show as higher request queue time. also check GC pauses in the proxy or serialization decode times if you're using gzip-protobuf.

[09:07] Marcos De la Cruz: check also initialization logs on the inference node — quantized kernel JITs sometimes compile lazily and show large one-off stalls on first long sequence.

[09:16] Luis Romero: we did collect traces from our side. i'll upload them to the shared folder.

[09:20] Eric Huang: perfect. once we have those we'll triage and run a focused stress test.

[09:27] Samira Patel: quick commercial note — if the outcome requires dedicated capacity with multi-az kv replication we can model cost and show projected unit economics. we'll aim to have a proposal after the benchmark run.

[09:38] Dr. Priya Anand: timeline wise, we're targeting an internal decision in three weeks; so your benchmarks and proposal will need to land within that window.

[09:45] Samira Patel: understood, we'll target results and a draft SOW within two weeks.

[09:50] Eric Huang: final quick recs from the SE side: 1) short-term — pre-warm top-100 prefixes, switch to msgpack serde for KV to reduce decode CPU, increase batch window to 40ms for heavy routes, 2) medium-term — replicate hot keys and colocate KV with on-prem inference if possible, 3) long-term — consider a small dedicated fleet for consistent tail SLOs, and use route-level adaptive batching.

[10:18] Marta Kovacevic: that sounds actionable. we'll try the serde change and provide logs in 48 hours.

[10:26] Samira Patel: excellent. let's recap next steps.

- Marta to share VPC/proxy configs and production traces.

[10:42] Dr. Priya Anand: thanks. great session.

[10:45] Samira Patel: thanks everyone. we'll follow up in the thread with artifacts.
